mercy_translation.text:
Since these things are so, and the demonstration concerning the resurrection of the body and the Savior's victory over death is clear, let us now refute the unbelief of the Jews and the mockery of the Greeks.

For perhaps on these matters the Jews disbelieve and the Greeks laugh, ridiculing what they regard as the unseemliness of the cross and the Word of God's becoming man. But our argument will not hesitate to proceed against both, especially since it possesses clear demonstrations against them.

The Jews who disbelieve can be refuted from the Scriptures which they themselves read, for from beginning to end and in every divinely inspired book these matters are taught plainly. The prophets from long before announced the wonder concerning the Virgin and the birth from her, saying: “Behold, the Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which translated means “God with us.”

Moses, who is truly great and is also believed by them to be truthful, recognized as weighty and true the saying concerning the Savior's becoming man and recorded it: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man from Israel, and he shall crush the rulers of Moab.” And again: “How beautiful are your houses, Jacob, your tents, Israel, like shaded valleys, like gardens beside rivers, like tents which the Lord has pitched, like cedars beside waters. A man shall come forth from his seed, and he shall rule over many nations.” And Isaiah says again: “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he shall take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians.”

That he will appear as a human being is proclaimed beforehand through these passages. But that the One who comes is Lord of all is again foretold when they say: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a swift cloud and shall come into Egypt, and the handmade things of Egypt shall be shaken.” From there the Father also calls him back, saying: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius now shifts into an extended scriptural apologetic addressed first to Jewish objections.
The biblical citations reflect the Septuagintal forms used by Athanasius and therefore sometimes differ from modern translations based on the Hebrew Masoretic text.
